### 5.1.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions: The Collapse of the Classical Civil Law's Geological Fault Line

The expanse of contemporary civil law stands today atop a profound epistemological geological fault line that threatens the doctrinal integrity built over centuries. When the codifiers of continental European civil law—who subsequently bequeathed this legal system to Indonesia via the principle of concordance—constructed the architecture of the law of obligations in the early nineteenth century, the world was envisioned as a mechanical space susceptible to rational prediction (Kotz, 2017). Legal relationships arose from clean, transparent obligations: between the free will of two legal subjects equal before the law based on the Principle of Consensualism (Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)), or through palpable unlawful acts where a human actor directly executed physical actions harming the person or property of another (Levenbach, 1934). Articles 1320 through 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) formulated free will (*wilsovereenstemming*) and the absence of vitiated consent, such as mistake (*dwaling*), duress (*bedreiging*), or fraud (*bedrog*), as the sacred pillars of contractual legitimacy. Meanwhile, Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) was designed to capture the physical vibrations of a wrongful act yielding tangible, mathematically calculable damages, deeply rooted in the school of subjective liability (*aansprakelijkheid op grond van schuld*) (Schwenzer et al., 2012).

However, when this private law confronts generative Artificial Intelligence systems, these epistemological foundations instantly collapse, akin to a sandcastle assaulted by the rising tide of computational cognitivism operating beyond the reach of human senses (Floridi, 2013). Genealogically, the doctrines of breach of contract (*wanprestasi*) and unlawful acts (*onrechtmatige daad*) heavily rely on a chain of linear causality empirically observable by human common sense, recalling John Searle's (1980) epistemological critique regarding the absence of true semantic understanding in artificial symbolic systems. If an individual fires a bullet, the projectile launches and tears through bodily tissue; if a negligent driver strikes a pedestrian, brake failure or visual distraction serves as tangible empirical evidence of fault (*schuld*). Yet, how are we to weigh the "fault" of a Large Language Model emitting streams of tokenized words laden with synthetic empathy, which gradually erodes an individual's psychological bulwark and drives them toward the brink of chronic despair or destructive acts, as analyzed in contemporary neuro-ethical studies (Farahany, 2023)? Herein lies the systemic failure of the classical legal school. An algorithm is neither a human possessing free will nor a corporation in a conventional form whose malicious intent (*mens rea*) can be readily identified (Calo, 2014). It is a cluster of mathematical parameters within a high-dimensional latent space that produces the illusion of emotional intimacy—a cold wax mask that nonetheless glows warmly in the eyes of the victim.

Modern legal epistemology remains trapped in an obsolete dichotomy between the material and the immaterial, between intentionality and mechanical negligence, even though Wiener (1950) warned long ago of the complexities of cybernetic feedback. When software acts as an "emotional companion" validating the dark ideation of a fragile user, the resulting harm is not a physical laceration of the skin, but the silent, invisible decay of cognitive architecture (Zuboff, 2019). Our civil law, with all its grandeur in regulating disputes over material objects, suddenly turns illiterate when confronted with psychological suffering generated by probability calculations of tokens. The endeavor to cram this digital harm into the narrow confines of Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) frequently culminates in a juridical dead end, as the elements of "fault" and "damage" forfeit their traditional empirical manifestations (Hogeveen, 2021). We are attempting to measure cosmic radiation using a colonial-era wooden caliper; the inevitable outcome is a failure of substantive justice enforcement that leaves victims lamenting in solitude without adequate compensatory protection. 

Furthermore, within the framework of conventional civil proof, the burden of proof (*onus probandi*) rests upon the plaintiff to establish the existence of fault and causal nexus—a burden nearly impossible to satisfy in the era of big data (Vandevelde, 2017). Within a tightly sealed technological ecosystem where trade secrets protect model architecture and weight optimization algorithms, the plaintiff faces an impenetrable bureaucratic and technical wall. Vitiated consent in digital contracts—for instance, when a consumer agrees to Terms of Service (ToS) laden with concealed exoneration clauses—no longer stems from simple mistakes (*dwaling*) as contemplated under Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*), but rather from architectural interface manipulations (*dark patterns*) that systematically subvert the cognitive autonomy of legal subjects (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Consequently, this crisis demands a radical overhaul of how we define legal subjects, objects of obligations, and parameters of fault in the era of cognitive disruption, aligning with the principle of human dignity protection mandated in modern instruments such as the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689).
